newsitem.title: USA: Apparel boosts retailers' November sales.
newsitem.headline: Apparel boosts retailers' November sales.

text.p: Strong apparel sales with fewer promotions cheered many retailers in November, but industry analysts said Thursday that consumer electronics continued to lag.
Calendar quirks made some year-to-year comparisons look negative because Thanksgiving was later this year, but analysts said that on a week-by-week basis, sales were strong.

"Everybody had been downplaying their expectations for November because of this calendar shift, and I actually think the numbers look pretty good," said Karen Sack, a retail analyst for Standard & Poor's.

Salomon Brothers noted that an improving retail environment for apparel, coupled with easier comparisons, led to gains in November sales. Its same-store sales index for the month rose 3.9 percent, compared with 2.9 percent a year ago.

"Concurrently, we believe that lower levels of discounting and strong inventory and expense controls have positioned the major retailers well in terms of profitability," Salomon analysts said in a report.

Sears, Roebuck and Co., for example, said it rang up record sales over the Thanksgiving weekend. Although sales at stores open at least a year fell 0.7 percent for the four weeks ended Nov. 30, Sears said the month went according to plan.

"Sales were on plan for November, given the fact that Thanksgiving was later this year," Sears Chairman Arthur Martinez said in a statement. "Record sales over Thanksgiving weekend produced an encouraging jump-start for a strong holiday shopping season at Sears."
However, consumer electronics retailers reported weaker performances, with sales at both Best Buy and Circuit City down a sharp 8 percent, while Tandy Corp.'s sales fell 2 percent.
Without a blockbuster product like last year's Windows 95 software, consumer electronics are lagging, analysts said.
"I think it's going to end up being one of the best years in the last four for apparel, and for consumer electronics one of the worst," said Dean Ramos, a retail analyst for Dain Bosworth Inc.
During the same period last year, Best Buy's comparable store sales rose 15 percent, the company said.
Wal-Mart Stores Inc., the nation's largest retailer, said its November same-store sales rose 4 percent, and Kmart Corp. sales climbed 4.4 percent.

J.C. Penney Co. Inc. said its sales gained 2.5 percent last month, while Dayton Hudson Corp., which operates department stores as well as the Target discount stores, said its November same-store sales rose 1.3 percent.
Those results, however, were pulled down by a 10.5 percent slide at its department stores and a 9 percent drop at its Mervyn's unit. Target sales gained 7 percent.
One notable exception was Gymboree Corp., which reported that November same-store sales slumped 15 percent. Its stock skidded $6.25, or nearly 23 percent, to $21.50 in morning trading on Nasdaq.

In the year-ago period, Gymboree had "a lot of markdowns and too much inventory," said Anita Gallitano, an analyst at Alex Brown. "This year, the inventory issue is not that great, but it's just not selling as well as expected."
The Thanksgiving holiday fell on Nov. 28 this year, while last year it was Nov. 23.
"Business is going well," said Richard Jaffe of Schroder Wertheim. "It look's like it'll be a strong holiday. Day-to-day business is good, with much less promotional and more regular pricing."
